slides.title: – Assume we have k classifiers M1, M2, …, Mk
slides.content: – Assume we have k classifiers M1, M2, …, Mk – Consider classifier M: – given a new instance x, M computes M1(x), M2(x), …, Mk(x), counts how often each class is predicted, and returns the class that is predicted most often – In other words: M lets all classifiers vote and returns the majority vote as its answer – How well will M work? slides.title: – The question is difficult to answer in general, but we can analyze what
slides.content: – The question is difficult to answer in general, but we can analyze what happens under some simplifying assumptions – Let us assume: 1. all classifiers M1, …, Mk have the same accuracy p 2. mistakes made by different classifiers are statistically independent - That is: for i≠j, P(Mi wrong | Mj wrong) = P(Mi wrong | Mj right) = P(mi is wrong) - Or: “if something is difficult for Mj, that doesn’t mean it’s also difficult for Mi ” Faculteit, departement, dienst … 17 Voting

slides.title: – Bagging works with any learner in principle
slides.content: – Bagging works with any learner in principle – Bagging works best for unstable learners – Learner is UNSTABLE if: minor variations in training data results in major changes in classifier output – Unstable: Decision trees, neural networks, rule learning algorithms, 1NN – Stable: Linear regression, kNN (k>1), linear threshold algorithms Faculteit, departement, dienst … 36 Sampling based ensembles

slides.title: – Typically, we want “strong learners”, i.e., high chance to get small error rate
slides.content: – Typically, we want “strong learners”, i.e., high chance to get small error rate – Boosting works with “weak learner”: Models are (slightly) better than random guessing – General approach – Learn an additive model – Greedily add a model at a time – Current model focuses on correcting mispredictions from the previous models Faculteit, departement, dienst … 60 Boosting

slides.title: – Works for binary classification problems
slides.content: – Works for binary classification problems – Learns additive model iteratively 𝐹𝑋= α1ℎ1(X)+α2ℎ2 𝑋+ ⋯+ α𝑡ℎ𝑡(𝑋) – Two big ideas when adding new model ℎ𝑡+1: – Idea 1: Weight examples that are classified incorrectly by ℎ𝑡 – Idea 2: Prediction is a weighted vote where more accurate models have a higher weight 𝛼 Faculteit, departement, dienst … 61 Adaboost

slides.content: Given: Training examples E, Integer T Give every example 𝑒∈𝐸equal weight we = 1 |𝐸| For t = 1 … T: Train a simple classifier ℎₜ using the current example weights 𝜀𝑡←σ 𝑒∈𝐸 ℎ𝑡𝑒≠𝑦𝑒 𝑤𝑒 Sum the weights of all incorrectly classified examples given labels 𝑦𝑒 𝛼𝑡= 1 2 ln( 1− 𝜀𝑡 𝜀𝑡) For every training example 𝑒∈𝐸: If ℎₜ classifies it incorrectly →Increase its weight 𝑤𝑒 Otherwise →Decrease its weight 𝑤𝑒 Normalize the example weights to 1: 𝑤𝑒= 𝑤𝑒 Σ𝑒∈𝐸𝑤𝑒 Add ℎₜ with voting strength 𝛼ₜ to the ensemble Faculteit, departement, dienst … 62 AdaBoost

slides.title: – Key idea: Error only measures if classification is correct, but confidence of
slides.content: – Key idea: Error only measures if classification is correct, but confidence of prediction is important – Measure confidence by margin: (weighted vote +) – (weighted vote - ) – Large margins mean more weak learners agree, hence more rounds does not necessarily imply that the final classifier is getting more complex – Theorem: Large margins yield better bound on generalization error Faculteit, departement, dienst … 70 Margins

slides.title: – Statistical sources
slides.content: – Statistical sources – Classifiers are “too local” and can easily fit the data (e.g., nearest neighbor, large decision trees) – Computational sources – Decision made on small subsets of the data (e.g., decision tree splits near the leaves) – Randomization in the learning algorithm (e.g., neural nets with random initial weights) – Unstable learning algorithms (e.g., decision boundary can change if one training example changes) – High variance ⇒model is overfitting the data Faculteit, departement, dienst … 95 Sources of Variance

slides.title: – Inherent randomness
slides.content: – Inherent randomness – Some processes are genuinely stochastic, such as equipment failure or customer behavior. – Unobserved variables – Important information is missing from the input features – Measurement error – Sensors, laboratory measurements or data-entry processes record imperfect values. – Ambiguous or inconsistent labels – Different experts may assign different labels to the same example. Faculteit, departement, dienst … 98 Sources of Noise

slides.title: – Typically:
slides.content: – Typically: – Bias: Do not have good hypotheses in the considered class – Variance: hypothesis class too big – Hence, we are faced with a trade-off: – More expressive hypothesis class, which generates higher variance – Less expressive class, which generates higher bias Faculteit, departement, dienst … 99 Bias variance tradeoff

slides.title: – Ensembles can address both bias and variance!
slides.content: – Ensembles can address both bias and variance! – Bagging – If bootstrap approximation is correct, then would reduce variance without changing bias – In practice, bagging can reduce both – For high-bias classifiers, can reduce bias – For high-variance classifiers, can reduce variance  – Boosting – Early iterations: primarily reduces bias – Later iterations: primarily reduces variance (apparently) Faculteit, departement, dienst … 100 Explanation 1: Bias-Variance

slides.title: – How can the learning algorithm select among set of (almost) equally good
slides.content: – How can the learning algorithm select among set of (almost) equally good hypotheses? – Bayes optimal classifier: Weighted majority vote of all hypotheses – Weighted by their posterior probability – Provably the best possible classifier, that is, minimizes the error rate – Ensemble learning approximates Bayes optimal Faculteit, departement, dienst … 106 Explanation 2: Statistical explanation

slides.title: – Most learning algorithms search through hypothesis space to find one “good”
slides.content: – Most learning algorithms search through hypothesis space to find one “good” model – Most interesting hypothesis spaces are: – Huge/infinite – Heuristic search is essential – Learner might get stuck in a local minimum – One strategy for avoiding local minima: Repeat the search many times with random restarts: This is similar to bagging!
